newsitem.title: THAILAND: Baht float set to hit exposed Thai debtors.
newsitem.headline: Baht float set to hit exposed Thai debtors.

text.p: Thai corporates with high unhedged foreign loan exposure are likely to face severe repayment problems as costs soar in the wake of the baht's managed float on Wednesday, bankers and analysts said.

Thai corporates have around $60-80 billion or the equivalent outstanding in foreign currency loans, with many unhedged against currency fluctuations after years when the baht was virtually fixed by the Bank of Thailand.
"Are Thai companies going to be able to repay their dollar loans is the next big question," one senior European analyst said.
"And if they can't, then the banks are going to have to take a big hit."
Thailand's central bank ended months of devaluation speculation on Wednesday when it decided to float the currency to help pull the country out of its biggest economic slump for more than a decade.
Previously, the baht was pegged to a basket of currencies dominated by the dollar.
The move saw the baht lose around 15-20 percent of its quoted value. Unprotected borrowers in foreign denominated debt now face a corresponding rise in loan repayment costs.
Financial authorities have pledged to help businesses hit by the baht's flotation, but there are fears some will be forced out of business by the added cost of currency exchange losses.
Analysts say firms among Thailand's fledgling telecommunications, petrochemicals, steel, cement and heavy industrial sectors are among the biggest borrowers in foreign currency.
The Thai commercial banks themselves have been heavy borrowers of foreign funds in recent years though legally most of their foreign exposure must be hedged.
Only two banks, Bank of Ayudhya Plc and First Bangkok City Bank Plc, had foreign denominated assets which exceeded their foreign denominated liabilities, analysts said.

"There are two things likely to affect the banks. The first is their ability to service their own borrowing, and the second is the possible deterioration in asset quality because of the potential difficulties clients may have repaying foreign denominated loans," said Andrew Maule, bank analyst at Vickers Ballas.

Many local brokers were busy assessing individual firms' exposure to possible foreign exchange losses though many said identifying which companies had hedged against currency fluctuations was difficult, analysts said.
But they warned the net affect on Thai corporates, most with only limited global spread, was likely to be severe.
"It's a very different case from the Swedish or British devaluations. Firms in those countries had high exposures to the global economy. Thailand has very limited exposure," said one foreign analyst.
While some sectors had a intrinsic protection against exchange losses, others were naturally exposed, analysts said.

"Some companies and sectors have a much better natural hedge than others to the extent that they are more or less part of the global economy, whereas say a retailer would have a very poor natural hedge," said Richard Henderson at Krungthai Thanakit.
Many fear the central bank -- which saw its foreign exchange reserves fall to a two-year low of $33 billion after defending the baht from speculation in May -- can do little to help.

With the International Monetary Fund, the Bank of Japan or other international central banks also pledging assistance to Thailand, analysts said the future for hard hit Thai firms may come down to the willingness and speed of these agencies to help.
